critiques: Duplicity ultimately comes off as a breath of fresh air amid a movie season rife with bleak horror films, hopelessly juvenile comedies and bloated superhero epics.
A tawdry cocktail of red herrings, cheap psychology, and shameless horror-movie tropes.
Shameless in its appropriation of incidents and atmosphere from earlier horror movies, with De Niro giving one of the emptier performances of his latter-day career.
Hide and Seek is the worst sort of horror film -- one that takes itself seriously without having anything to back up that attitude.
"Trauma causes pain" - but what about the intense psychobabble in this horror-thriller?
An elaborate equation consisting entirely of bad horror tropes and trashy psychological symbolism.
It was really only a matter of time before 10-year-old Dakota Fanning brought her unsettling precocity to the horror genre. And it's a bit of a waste.
It may be an efficient horror exercise, but not an exercise you'll much enjoy participating in.
The result is more campy than scary, and in the horror game, that means nobody wins.

Once upon a time, horror pictures like this one played urban grind houses and starred the B-movie likes of Wings Hauser. The gloss of A-list casting and slicked-up production values doesn't necessarily serve them well.

Another of those real-estate horror movies that sticks it to urbanites who overspend on picturesque Victorian houses in towns where the locals resent them. For city folk in rambling country homes, something wicked this way comes.
Check it out if you like the horror genre. It was not bad at all.
The most chilling horror movie of the year.
Why bother with horror films when you can see this?
Villeneuve and screenwriter Taylor Sheridan aren't selling more than a tautological action movie with the dread and body count of a horror film.
By the end, it packs a death stare so potent it will make you want to turn a blind eye to the shadowy brutality of its real-world horrors.

Catching Fire is best in its first hour, when it concentrates on the politics and the specific horrors of Panem. It becomes more conventional in the second half and loses steam, but it's always heading somewhere.
On one level, the documentary Jesus Camp is all about evangelical Christians keeping up with the terrorists.
As a documentary, Jesus Camp could lose its haunted-house score and contrapuntal Air America refrains and still deliver its message...
This startling documentary -- a voyage deep into the culture of American evangelical Christianity -- is a superior species of agitprop.
The compassionate god of love so evident in the Sermon on the Mount is nowhere to be found in the documentary JESUS CAMP
The scariest movie of the season by far...a fine, thought-provoking documentary.
Effective documentary, if somewhat repetitious.
A frightening, infuriating, yet profoundly compassionate documentary about the indoctrination of children by the Evangelical right.
This riveting documentary explores Kids on Fire, a summer camp in Devils Lake, N.D., that grooms children to be soldiers in 'God's army'.
No matter your religious or political affiliation (or lack thereof), this supremely even-handed documentary from Heidi Ewing and Rachel Grady is cinematic dynamite.

While it could be argued that this somewhat chilling documentary sets out to make some of its subjects appear foolish, the film does allow them to speak clearly and at length, with next to no editorializing.
A brave, thoughtful documentary.
This unabashedly liberal documentary tries to redress the balance by giving the rest of America a wake up call: not all scary fundamentalists come strapped with explosives.

Flawed editing and intrusive and irritating commentary hardly detract from the shock value of this disturbing documentary. Compulsory viewing for anyone in the least bit concerned about religious extremism.
A smashingly exciting sci-fi adventure that ranks among the very best in the long-running Paramount franchise.
If the film itself is a little bit generic, more of a popcorn sci-fi action film than a faithful adaptation of the characters from the series, that's probably all to the good.

For non-Trekkers, this is a great, free-standing special-effects adventure with much more fleshy characters than your average sci-fi yarn. Definitely a good ride. But there are also plenty of nods to Star Trek aficionados.
The story is typical sci-fi fantasy, but the conviction of the cast--most notably the always-phenomenal Stewart--makes you believe and care.
District B-13 is bad sci-fi, but it succeeds as mindless action.
Francis Lawrence has crafted a gripping, richly textured sci-fi thriller with reams of underlying dystopian subtext.
Catching Fire is unvarnished sci-fi commentary on the present-day declination of our middle and lower social stratum and the moral indifference of the powerful and wealthy to their plight.
Catching Fire is a work of thoughtful, emotionally engaging sci-fi - everything that its predecessor The Hunger Games was not.
The new "The Empire Strikes Back," a smashing sci-fi sequel that takes its blockbuster franchise into deeper, smarter, more dramatically engaging territory.
...a well-crafted and superbly acted sci-fi dystopia that resonates with much of what's happening in our current age.
Enchanting drama based on a children's classic.
Is this a fun, flirty romantic comedy? A farce? A serious drama about espionage? When writer/director Tony Gilroy figures it out, will someone let me know?
A timely, brisk, and witty combination love story and drama about corporate malfeasance.
Thoroughly delightful, invigorating and captivating with just the right balance of drama and comedy.
With a less than stirring performance by Robert De Niro, this one will leave seasoned psychodrama fans underwhelmed.
It has the melodrama of other episodes of the films but fewer absurdities this time around.
A tender Israeli drama with a gorgeous soundtrack and a truly sympathetic character at its heart ...
The movie succumbs to maudlin sentiment and melodrama that Lennon himself might have dismissed with one of his signature cutting remarks.

There are brief moments when Nowhere Boy takes your breath away, when the frisson of future knowledge sends a shiver down the spine. But they're outweighed by the melodrama and the politesse of this disappointingly toothless biopic.

Visual artist Sam Taylor-Wood casts aside her moody conceptual art and directs a lively, insightful and slightly nostalgic look at the drama of John Lennon's formative years and his relationship with the two women who brought him up.
Moviegoers who don't care about The Beatles may skip it and miss out on a subtle coming-of-age drama that stands on its own merits, notably Aaron Johnson's evocation of Lennon as an angry young man.

In contrast to so many other salutes to the Beatles and their legacy, this intimate drama focuses on John Lennon's turbulent teenage years, not just referencing, but explaining so much of what, later, showed up in his music.
More a reasonably absorbing domestic drama than a biopic of young John Lennon.
It's a pleasant-enough creation story to revisit, one weighted down by melodrama and lifted up by some rocking tunes.
Anchored by a strong central turn, Nowhere Boy crafts entertaining, small-scale drama out of Lennon's huge-sized legend. It just lacks the spark and ambition of its subject.
Places a huge burden on [Aaron] Johnson, who has to play an icon in his pre-icon days while holding down the center of a family drama about a boy with abandonment issues.
Occasionally energetic, but primarily frantic, Boy appears more fascinated with melodrama than investigation, mashing down Lennon?s surprisingly complex adolescence into a flavorless paste.
Works as a conventionally satisfying docu-drama about the difficult teen years of a musical legend. If only it could have been as unconventional as Lennon was.
Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid (1969) is the likeably entertaining, charming and amusing comedy/drama of the friendship and camaraderie shared between

"Sicario" features neither the twistiness of "Prisoners" nor the weirdness of "Enemy," and so is just a very solid procedural that eschews bigger drama in favor of a continual slow build... to nowhere in particular.
Seductive and playful, this corporate espionage thriller has a breezy attitude that keeps us thoroughly engaged through all of the twists and turns of the plot.
A beautifully shot, well written and impressively acted thriller that's both suspenseful and emotionally engaging.
In top form, Julia Roberts and Clive Owen star in this sexy, witty, elegant romantic thriller made for mature audiences.

A high-tech romantic thriller set in the little-seen world of corporate espionage, Tony Gilroy's second feature is sophisticated adult entertainment which puts the lazy Ocean's films to shame with its clever writing, lively direction and visual panache.

Whatever the onscreen dilemma for Clive Owen's Ray and Julia Roberts' Claire, for us, it's a no-brainer. This slick and persuasive crime thriller has so much chemistry and chutzpah; we're hooked from the start
The globetrotting spy thriller never measures up to being first-rate.
It's good to see an espionage thriller that avoids the clichés of the genre.
A perfectly-crafted espionage thriller married to the best throwback rom-com in years.
Clever, complex romantic thriller is too twisty for tweens.
An ordinary, mildly suspenseful, eventually preposterous thriller that warrants no more attention or thought than the time it takes to watch it, if that.
I jumped twice in Hide and Seek, but John Polson's new thriller has only a good, but painfully wasted cast to recommend it.
A psychological thriller that dangles over the precipitous edge of awfulness a full 90 minutes before toppling into that abyss with the resounding clatter of Robert De Niro's ham-on-rye overacting.
Not the supernatural thriller you might be hoping for.
An absorbing mystery-thriller for its first hour ... until it races off the tracks toward a dumb, albeit predictable, twist ending.
Hide and Seek really isn't a suspense thriller at all. It's a mystery movie. It's always a mystery when highly talented people commit the time and effort to a film that is so obviously mediocre.

The second half gets downright silly as the country home turns into a slaughterhouse. What could have been a Sixth Sense-style intelligent thriller heads straight for the drive-in, though it's still handled with considerable skill.
A nifty little thriller with some effective psychological and supernatural flourishes.
Hide and Seek is a technically slicker paranoid thriller than director John Polson's previous Swimfan, but its esteemed posture makes it even trashier.
It's a genuine scare-fest that will have you squirming in your seat and even screaming aloud. Hide and Seek is the best little psychological thriller in a long while.
An absorbing, understated thriller until it totally self-destructs in the final reel with a twist we've seen too many times in recent years.
Ultra sleek, cool, stylish and smart filmmaking. Supremely sophisticated fun - but better pay close attention.
This thriller's flashback scenes interrupted the story's flow too much for me. But Julia Roberts and Clive Owen are fun to watch.
You simply haven't had this much fun at the multiplex in a long, long time.

Much of the fun is all about what's 'in play'--acting--from the spy and lover roles these characters may or may not be playing and which sides (personal, professional) they're playing for or against, to our assumptions about these stars' personas.
Duplicity is a light and airy affair that has far too much fun with zingy one-liners to be concerned with the rather relevant dirty laundry that's being aired out.
It's pretty fun and entertaining for the most part. However, it gets a little talky and ends with a plot twist that's perhaps too convoluted and contrived for its own good.
Gilroy and his stars make it elegant fun to be fooled, but they sure as hell make you work for it.

Duplicity is entertaining, but the complexities of its plot keep it from being really involving. The fun is in watching Roberts and Owen fencing with dialogue, keeping straight faces, trying to read each other's minds.
Slick, sneaky, snarky fun - a devilish double-cross
Drew Barrymore's directorial debut blasts in some girls who just want to have fun - and you'll be happy to join them.
[It's] hard not to be moved by the irrepressible sense of fun and optimism on display here.
Drew Barrymore's directorial debut is an energetic celebration of grrrl power, and it sure is fun to watch.
...a fun female-empowerment movie that marks an impressively crowd-pleasing directorial debut for Drew Barrymore.
Whip It looks like it was a fun movie to make. Unfortunately, it's not all that fun to watch.
Girls just wanna have fun -- and boy, do they as rough 'n' ready roller derby players -- in Whip It, Drew Barrymore's exuberant and totally winning directing debut.
Even if a tale of female empowerment through roller derby is not your particular cup of tea, Barrymore delivers it with such a giddy good sense of fun that it's easy enough to go along with.
A small-scale movie that feels like it was a lot of fun to make. It has a rambunctious charm, a considerable amount of heart and a steady supply of laughs.
Barrymore gently sells the niceness of it all. It turns out that roller girls just wanna have fun and that the sisterhood of the traveling skates is one big happy family.
Drew Barrymore has successfully directed a generally fun roller derby movie that never loses sight that the main character's journey should always be kept front and center.
Hide and Seek is trashy, but there's no fun to be had in its ugly child-endangerment psychoses....The hidden-in-plain-sight "secret": another crappy movie.
